Voatdev

Last week in /v/voatdev there was a request for a feature enabling users to replace certain words or phrases with other words or phrases. Putt responded by saying the prototype for such functionality already exists, and that one day users will be able to create such replacement sets and even subscribe to the replacement sets of others. This kind of feature is commonly referred to as a "word filter" on the chans, and it is widely looked down upon. I share this negative sentiment; however, the controversy emerges from such word filters existing sitewide or subverse wide, imposed from above, so to speak. This enables censorship of certain topics, or can at least make it much more difficult to discuss certain issues. But if such functionality remains entirely voluntary and accessible on an individual-by-individual basis, I see no problem with it, personally. This is another example of a feature that gives the users more power and freedom, not less, while remaining entirely optional.

There was also a report about anonymous posts still upticking the number of submissions figure on user profiles, thus connecting anonymous content to usernames in some remote way. As I understand it, this was not always the case, and it is considered a bug and will be addressed.

The OP states what I think was a reasonable and defensible opinion that legitimizing or tolerating those who explicitly called for violence (not necessary against anyone in particular) could threaten the ability of Voat to survive as a platform. The post was likely inspired by the recent actions taken against Gab for hosting content that was inciting of violence, specifically from a person who later went on to act violently.

One rebuttal to this is that other, more mainstream platforms host violent content all the time and face no consequences for it, Facebook and twitter not least among them. There are countless tweets inciting violence against people, including the President of the United States, and yet twitter faces no existential threats. Likewise, Facebook has allowed rapes and hostage situations to be livestreamed on their platform, but no one has proposed that Facebook be taken down. Is this because these platforms are much larger than the likes of Gab or Voat, or is it because the "right" people are having violence incited (or acted) against them?

Another point that must be considered is the undeniably critical role that violence has played in human history. The West has evolved in many ways over a long period of time, and part of that evolution has been a disdain for violence. Thomas Hobbes defined the fundamental law of human nature to be the seeking of peace, for without peace, survival cannot be assured, and without survival nothing else can follow. Working in ways that help people survive are to be held as preferable to maintaining a state of chaos (or war) in which survival is not readily assured. It seems that the West's disdain for violence is well-founded, then.

Yet at the same time, a major contributing factor (I do not think it would be superfluous to say the most critical contributing factor) to our survival has been our ancestors' willingness to be violent, to act brutally, when the cause was deemed necessary. Whether we like it or not, our present existence depends entirely on the totally brutal, cruel, and perhaps, to our own eyes, evil actions of those who came before us. Violence is inseparable from humanity so long as humanity is inseparable from the material realm itself. It is worth noting that Hobbes' fundamental law came with a caviat:

And consequently it is a precept, or general rule of reason that every man ought to endeavour peace, as far as he has hope of obtaining it; and when he cannot obtain it, that he may seek and use all helps and advantages of war. The first branch of which rule containeth the first and fundamental law of nature, which is to seek peace and follow it. The second, the sum of the right of nature, which is by all means we can to defend ourselves.

So almost four hundred years ago one of our cleverest ancestors understood that part of maintaining peace is going to war, because in a world as complex and chaotic as ours, there are sure to be interests that conflict, sure to be those who violate a person's or a group's conception of justice, sure to be those who provoke violence in one form or another. In order to ensure we adhere to the fundamental law of human nature, in order to be sure we seek peace for the sake of our survival, sometimes all the helps and advantages of war must be employed.

So I can fully understand why an issue such as this was controversial on Voat. On one hand, I do not want to see anyone innocent get hurt, and oftentimes, in our rage and fear, we advocate violence against those who are perhaps innocent, or at least indistinguishable from ourselves in their complicity. On the other hand, there are times when we may find ourselves in a position where forces greater and more daring than ourselves are already employing the advantages of war against us, and if we hope to survive we will have no choice but to do the same.

Inciting violence remains illegal in the United States of America, where Voat is based, and so doing so, especially explicitly against identifiable individuals or groups, will give those who wish to destroy us the legal grounds to do so. Whether no actions are taken against others more powerful than us to allow content much worse is irrelevant to the eyes of our enemies. Regardless of our feelings about our present situation, if we want this freedom platform of ours, which has helped so many of us, given us so much, for so little in return, then I suggest we hold our tongues -- but sharpen our minds and our defences -- where such notions are concerned.

Voat Updates

As mentioned above, Putt made an announcement last week, in which he admitted to making two changes to Voat without first consulting the userbase. Putt's self-awareness and good intentions in coming forward with such a confession should be noted, even if he was pressured to do so.

The second change he mentioned I think barely required an apology -- a change was mistakenly made to Voat, and upon noticing this, he reverted it back to where he was. Still, by this point some users had become familiar with the mistaken state of affairs, and were put off by the switch back to olden ways that they never knew.

It is the first change he made that I think was most important. Most users responding to the announcement, at least that I saw, seemed to react maturely and with understanding, which is always nice to see. Again contrary to tradition, there was very little misunderstanding or manufactured outrage. To manually flair posts containing racial slurs as NSFW in the interest of hiding said posts only from those who choose to have such content hidden seems a reasonable thing. Some points were raised, however, that I view as worth repeating.

  • Division of NSFW content
  • User awareness

Voat Banlog

No users were banned last week.

No domains were banned last week.

Stay vigilant, goats.

• Many people (including myself) have traditionally disabled NSFW content for the sake of removing pornographic material from our feeds, but have no issue with reading racial slurs (whether we agree with their usage or not), and would prefer to not have such content hidden, while we would still like to hide pornographic material. The ability to hide one type of content but not the other would be much preferred. A user mentioned this point within the announcement thread, and Putt responded suggesting that such a differentiation would be "discussed", and before changes were made. (I hope Putt does not take away from this situation that he must consult the userbase before every little change, especially changes that do nothing but gives users more power. In my opinion, the only reason this case should have had a discussion, or really just an announcement first, was that those who had NSFW content disabled for the sake of hiding pornographic material suddenly had ordinary posts with curse words in them disappear from their feed).

I think the user can enable the NSFW setting but disable the thumbnails setting as a workaround. I have both enabled, but have not seen much pornographic thumbnails while browsing /v/all list. It might just be the default setting of /v/all or that I have blocked enough of those subverses.

That is an option, but it would be a shame to disable all thumbnails just for that purpose. I have enough NSFW subverses blocked that I eventually re-enabled NSFW, so blocking the subverses themselves is an option, yes.

• The default setting when creating an account seems to be that NSFW content is disabled (users have to manually check a box in their accounts settings in order to enable such content). While I think that is fine as a default, I also think that, if content is going to be hidden by default, users should be made aware of that as clearly as possible upon account registration. For example, a pop-up after registration stating something along the lines of "Please note: by default NSFW content is disabled (hidden from your front page). This includes pornographic material and submissions containing racial slurs. If you wish to unhide such content, check the applicable box in your user profile".
